abstract: Understanding the mechanisms linking stringent climate policy and macro-financial risk is crucial for the effective mitigation of climate risks. This study uses panel data from 75 countries for the period 1995–2021 by applying a two-way fixed-effects model as a benchmark and performing various robustness tests. Moreover, it investigates the moderating roles of adaptation readiness and institutional quality in mitigating macro-financial risk, while analyzing heterogeneity based on both economic development levels and population size. This study systematically examines the impact of stringent climate policy on macro-financial risk and identifies several key findings. First, stringent climate policies have a significantly positive effect on reducing macro-financial risks. Second, the mitigating effect of stringent climate policies on macro-financial risks is primarily observed in debt risks and exchange rate risks, with a limited impact on liquidity, balance of payments, and inflation risks. Third, the mitigating effect of stringent climate policies is more pronounced in three sectors: food, ecosystem services, and infrastructure. Fourth, the analysis of the moderation channels demonstrates that effective levels of adaptation readiness and institutional quality can significantly enhance the risk-mitigation effect of stringent climate policies. Fifth, heterogeneity analysis reveals that stringent climate policy has a more significant impact on macro-financial risk in economically developed countries and countries with smaller populations. This study enhances our understanding of how stringent climate policies mitigate macro-financial risks and offers theoretical insights into effective risk prevention and mitigation strategies.
